questions.stem: Helen, 24, has migraine with aura. Before each attack she gets about 20 minutes of jumbled lines and bright dots, and then the headache starts. Her GP is prescribing sumatriptan 50 mg for severe attacks. What is the best instruction to give her about when to take it?
options: As soon as the visual symptoms begin, before any headache starts
At the start of the headache, once the visual symptoms have passed
Only once paracetamol has failed to help within 4 hours
Every morning during exam weeks to stop attacks starting
questions.why: Triptans work best when taken early in the headache phase. Taken during the aura, they do not prevent the headache and work less well. So tell her to take it as soon as the pain begins, once the aura has finished.
notes: Taking a triptan during the aura does not stop the headache developing, and it may not work as well. The dose should wait until the pain starts.
Waiting hours for simple analgesia to fail lets the attack become established. A triptan works best taken early in the headache, and it can be used first-line for severe attacks.
Triptans are acute treatments, not preventives. Taking them daily risks medication-overuse headache. Prevention uses drugs such as propranolol, amitriptyline or pizotifen.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, has migraine with typical visual aura. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill correctly for 3 years. She does not smoke, her repeat BP is 124/78, and her urine hCG is negative. She wants to stay on reliable contraception. What is the best plan for her contraception?
options: Continue the combined pill, as she is young, normotensive and a non-smoker
Change to a combined pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinylestradiol
Stop the combined pill and start a progestogen-only method today, with no gap
Take the combined pill continuously, skipping the hormone-free week
questions.why: Migraine with aura at any age is an absolute contraindication to oestrogen-containing contraception (UKMEC 4) because of the risk of ischaemic stroke. Switch her straight to a progestogen-only method (implant, LNG-IUD, POP or injection) or a copper IUD, with no gap in protection.
notes: Aura alone makes the combined pill UKMEC 4, whatever her age, BP or smoking status. Her other low-risk features do not make it safe.
Any dose of oestrogen is contraindicated in migraine with aura. A lower-dose ethinylestradiol pill still carries the added stroke risk.
Continuous dosing is sometimes used for menstrual migraine without aura. She is still taking oestrogen, so it remains contraindicated.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, describes bright dots and jumbled lines that start in one part of her vision. They spread slowly over about 20 minutes and then go completely before her throbbing headache begins. Which mechanism best explains this slowly spreading visual aura?
options: A slow wave of neuronal depolarisation spreading across the occipital cortex
Transient spasm of the cerebral arteries causing occipital lobe ischaemia
Small emboli passing through the retinal artery and briefly blocking flow
Trigeminal nerve fibres releasing CGRP around the meningeal blood vessels
questions.why: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depression: a wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation that moves across the visual cortex at about 2 to 5 mm/min, followed by a period of suppressed activity. Its slow speed explains why symptoms spread over 5 minutes or more and are positive at first.
notes: The old vascular theory has been replaced. The reduced blood flow during aura follows the neuronal wave and stays above ischaemic thresholds, and ischaemia gives negative, not spreading positive, symptoms.
Retinal emboli cause sudden, monocular, negative loss of vision (amaurosis fugax). They do not cause positive phenomena that spread slowly across the visual field.
Activation of trigeminal fibres with CGRP release explains the headache pain (the target of triptans and CGRP drugs), not the visual aura.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, has throbbing migraine pain over her left forehead. The pain comes from activated sensory fibres supplying the supratentorial dura and the large blood vessels inside it. Which nerve carries these fibres and explains why the pain is felt in the forehead?
options: Greater occipital nerve, from the dorsal ramus of C2
Meningeal branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)
questions.why: The supratentorial dura and large intracranial vessels are supplied mainly by V1 (the trigeminovascular system). Pain from them is therefore referred to the V1 dermatome: the forehead, the area around the eye and the front of the scalp.
notes: The greater occipital nerve supplies the back of the scalp, and C2 contributes to the posterior fossa dura. Pain from these sources is felt at the back of the head, not the forehead.
The facial nerve is mainly a motor nerve to the muscles of facial expression. It carries no meaningful sensory supply to the supratentorial dura.
Meningeal branches of the vagus supply the dura of the posterior fossa. Pain from there is referred to the ear and the back of the head, not the forehead.
